title: The last four: ه و ء ا

bigIdea.text: Four letters finish the alphabet: ه (ha), a soft breath from deep in the throat; و (waw), a 'w' or a long 'oo'; ء (hamza), a clean catch in the throat; and ا (alif), which stretches the vowel before it.

proper.text: ه changes shape the most: standing alone it is a small round ه, at the start هـ, in the middle ـهـ, at the end ـه. و is a small loop with a tail curving below the line. ء is a small mark that sits on the line or on a seat (أ ؤ ئ); the seat is not read, only the hamza. ا is a plain upright stroke. و and ا never join the letter after them.

Sounds: ه is a soft, open breath like the 'h' in 'hat'. و is 'w' as in 'wet', with rounded lips, never 'v'; a و with no vowel after a damma stretches the 'u' into a long 'oo'. ء is a clean catch in the throat, like the break in 'uh-oh'. ا never takes a vowel of its own: after a fatha it stretches the 'a' into a long 'aa'.

Sifat: ه is whispered (hams) and soft (rakhawa). ء is strong (shiddah: its sound stops fully) and holds the breath back (jahr). A و with sukun after a fatha has 'ease' (leen): it is said smoothly, without strain.

provenance.title: صفة حرف (العربية) (Sifat of Arabic letters) — Arabic Wikipedia

proper.text: Heavy or light: ه, و and ء are light. ا has no weight of its own: it sounds heavy after a heavy letter and light after a light one.

Common mistakes. Persian/Urdu readers: و said as 'v', and ه mixed up with ح. English speakers: English never ends a syllable with 'h', so a ه at the end of a syllable fades away; a ء between two vowels gets blurred instead of a clean catch; and long vowels are cut short.

points.detail: Deepest part of the throat, nearest the chest (shared with ه)
Deepest part of the throat, nearest the chest (shared with ء)
As a consonant: between the two lips (shared with ب and م)
As a long vowel (madd letter): the open space of the mouth and throat
Always a long vowel (madd letter): the open space of the mouth and throat

memoryHook.text: Ha breathes, hamza catches, waw rounds, alif stretches.

extras.text: Two more shapes appear at the ends of words: ى looks like ي without dots, and ة looks like ه with two dots (ta marbuta). They get their own lesson later.
A few letters in the mushaf are written but not read; they carry a small 'zero' sign. That sign gets its own lesson later.

note.text: Starts with hamza on a seat (أ); later a و after a damma.

drills.prompt: Say each letter with a fatha: هَ وَ ءَ
Waw with rounded lips, teeth off the lip (never 'v'): وَ وِ وُ

tip.text: Both come from the deepest part of the throat. ه is an open breath that flows. ء is a sudden catch that stops.

questions.q: Which letter changes its shape the most between the start, middle and end of a word?
explain: Right: ha has four quite different forms.
alif is always an upright stroke.
waw keeps its loop and tail.
dal keeps its corner.

questions.q: Where are ء and ه made?
options: The deepest part of the throat, nearest the chest
The part of the throat nearest the mouth
explain: Right.
That is the place of ع and ح.
That is the place of غ and خ.
That is the place of ب, م and و.

questions.q: How is و said as a consonant?
options: Only as 'oo', never as a consonant
explain: Right.
'v' puts the teeth on the lip; that is a Persian/Urdu habit to drop.
'f' is the letter ف.
With its own vowel, waw is the consonant 'w'.

questions.q: What does ا do after a fatha?
options: Adds a vowel of its own
Makes a catch in the throat
explain: Right: alif lengthens the fatha before it.
alif never carries a vowel of its own.
A catch is hamza, not alif.
After a fatha, alif is read as length (unless a small 'zero' sign marks it silent — a later lesson).

questions.q: Which letter of this group is strong (shiddah: its sound stops fully)?
explain: Right: hamza is one of the strong letters (أجد قط بكت).
ha is soft: its sound flows.
waw is soft: its sound flows.
alif is a long vowel: its sound flows.

questions.q: Persian and Urdu readers often say و like…
explain: Right: Arabic waw is 'w' (or a long 'oo'), never 'v'.
'b' closes the lips completely; waw only rounds them.
'f' is the letter ف.
'y' is the letter ي.

questions.q: In أ, hamza sits on a seat. What do you read?
options: Only the hamza, with its vowel; the seat is silent
Both the seat and the hamza
explain: Right: the seat just carries the hamza.
The seat is not read.
The seat is not read; the hamza is.
The hamza is read with its vowel.

questions.q: Which letter of this group is whispered (hams: the breath flows)?
explain: Right: ha is in the whispered group.
hamza holds the breath back (jahr).
waw is not in the whispered group.
alif is not in the whispered group.

questions.q: Where do the long vowels (madd letters) come from?
options: The open space of the mouth and throat (al-jawf)
explain: Right: that is why they are called the jawf letters.
waw as a consonant uses the lips, but the long vowels come from the jawf.
The nasal passage carries the hum of ن and م.
The tongue tip makes letters like ت, د and ن.

questions.q: Which quality does a و with sukun after a fatha have?
options: Ease (leen): it is said smoothly, without strain
explain: Right: leen belongs to و and ي with sukun after a fatha.
The whistle belongs to ص ز س.
The bounce belongs to ق ط ب ج د.
Repetition belongs to ر.

questions.q: Which pair of letters never join the letter after them?
explain: Right: waw and alif join only the letter before them.
ha and mim join on both sides.
ha joins on both sides (a hamza on the line joins neither).
kaf and lam join on both sides.

questions.q: Some London accents drop the 'h' in 'hat'. Why does that matter for ه?
options: ه is a real letter: leaving it out changes the word
It does not matter: ه is silent
ه is only a spelling mark
explain: Right: say every ha, even softly.
ha is pronounced.
ha is a full letter, not a mark.
Both are letters; each must be said.
Right: that is ta marbuta.
That is ى.
There is no such letter.
That is أ.

remnote: ه (ha) == Many shapes (ه هـ ـهـ ـه); deepest part of the throat; soft open breath; light
و (waw) == Loop with a tail; 'w' with rounded lips (never 'v'); after a damma, a long 'oo'
ء (hamza) == Small mark, alone or on a seat (أ ؤ ئ); deepest part of the throat; a clean catch
ا (alif) == Upright stroke; never takes its own vowel; after a fatha, a long 'aa'
Madd letters == ا, و after a damma, ي after a kasra; from the open space of the mouth and throat (al-jawf)
